job.style: a short story where children solve a real problem

passage: Rohan and Meera were helping their teacher decorate the classroom for the annual math fair. They decided to arrange colorful paper triangles in a row to create a beautiful border. Rohan noticed that for one triangle, they needed 3 sticks. For two triangles, they needed 6 sticks. Meera observed that the number of sticks is always 3 times the number of triangles. She wrote this as 3n, where n is the number of triangles. Rohan asked if n could be 4. Meera nodded, explaining that 3n means 3 multiplied by n, so for 4 triangles, they would need 12 sticks. Rohan then placed 5 blue sticks and 5 red sticks on the table. He said, 'If I call the blue sticks b and the red sticks r, then b plus r equals 10.' Meera agreed, noting that even though b and r are different letters, they could both represent the number 5. They realized that letters are just placeholders for numbers. Later, they saw a sign saying 'x plus 5 equals 10'. Meera explained that because it has an equals sign, it is an equation, unlike just writing x plus 5. They felt proud to use algebra to solve their decoration puzzle.

items.evidence: Meera observed that the number of sticks is always 3 times the number of triangles.
items.q: Rohan and Meera want a border of 7 triangles. How many sticks will they need?
items.explain: The sticks are always 3 times the triangles, so 7 triangles need 3 × 7 = 21 sticks.

wrong.why: adds the difference 3 instead of multiplying by 3
writes 3 and 7 side by side as 73
thinks the letter always stands for 10

items.evidence: Meera nodded, explaining that 3n means 3 multiplied by n, so for 4 triangles, they would need 12 sticks.
items.q: Rohan puts n = 4 into 3n. How should he work out its value?
items.explain: 3n means 3 multiplied by n, so when n is 4, 3n is 3 × 4 = 12.

wrong.why: puts the digits side by side
mixes up 3n with 3 more than n
squares n instead of multiplying by 3

items.evidence: Meera agreed, noting that even though b and r are different letters, they could both represent the number 5.
items.q: Rohan has 5 blue sticks (b) and 5 red sticks (r). What is true about b and r?
options: They must stand for different numbers
They stand for colours, not numbers
items.explain: Different letters can still stand for the same number, so b and r can both be 5.

wrong.why: thinks different letters must mean different numbers
thinks a letter stands for an object, like apples

items.evidence: Meera explained that because it has an equals sign, it is an equation, unlike just writing x plus 5.
items.q: Why is 'x + 5 = 10' called an equation, but 'x + 5' is not?
options: Only the first has an equals sign
Only the first uses a letter
Only the first adds a number
Only the first makes x stand for 10
items.explain: An equation must have an equals sign; x + 5 alone has no equals sign, so it is not one.

wrong.why: thinks any expression with a letter is an equation
thinks the plus sign makes an equation

items.evidence: They realized that letters are just placeholders for numbers.
items.q: Meera writes 5a. What does the letter a stand for?
options: A number, like a box to fill
A number fixed for every problem
The same as a times a
items.explain: Letters are placeholders for numbers, so a is a box where any number can go.

wrong.why: thinks the letter a stands for apples
thinks a letter has one fixed value forever
mixes up repeated adding with squaring
